nameStory: The Painted Suillus gets its artistic name from its striking appearance that looks like nature's own artwork. The cap's dark red surface is dramatically cracked and split, revealing bright yellow underneath like paint peeling away to show a different color beneath. It's as if someone took a paintbrush and created a beautiful crackled finish on this woodland mushroom.
description: The Painted Suillus is a medium-sized mushroom with a distinctive cracked, two-toned cap that makes it one of the most recognizable fungi in New England's pine forests. The cap starts deep red when fresh and develops a network of yellow cracks as it matures, creating a stunning mosaic pattern. Instead of gills, it has tiny yellow pores on the underside that turn brownish with age. The stem is sturdy and bears a grayish ring, often covered in soft hairs or scales.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Dark red surface that's dry to the touch, covered with hair-like scales separated by bright yellow cracks creating a distinctive crackled paint effect

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Small, angular yellow pores instead of gills on the underside, turning brownish as the mushroom ages

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy stem with a grayish cottony ring and soft hairs or scales covering the surface

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found growing from soil near eastern white pine trees, never on wood or other substrates

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, pleasant mushroomy scent without any strong or unpleasant odors

habitat: Look for Painted Suillus growing from the ground in mixed and coniferous forests where eastern white pines are present, as they form a vital partnership with these trees' roots. They prefer well-drained, acidic soils typical of New England's pine forests and can be found from lowland areas to moderate elevations. You'll often spot them scattered or in small groups near the base of mature white pines or in nearby clearings.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found fruiting during spring months as soil temperatures are still too cool for active growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season begins in early summer when warm, humid conditions and summer rains create ideal growing conditions. Look for fresh specimens with the most vibrant red and yellow coloration.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting through autumn until hard frosts arrive, though caps may appear more weathered and faded. Fall specimens often show more pronounced browning of the pores.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting occurs during winter months when the ground is frozen and the mycorrhizal partner trees are dormant.

funFact: The Painted Suillus is like an underground internet connector for pine forests – its fungal threads form a vast network that not only feeds the mushroom but also helps pine trees communicate with each other, sharing nutrients and even warning signals about insect attacks!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other Suillus species like S. decipiens, but the Painted Suillus is the only one with that distinctive red cap covered in yellow cracks. Memory trick: 'Painted' means colorful cracks – no other bolete in our region has this dramatic crackled paint job.
contextualKnowledge: This species has had a confusing taxonomical history and you may see it listed in older field guides as Suillus pictus, which is essentially the same mushroom with a different scientific name. The name changes don't affect identification – it's still the same distinctive crackled-cap mushroom.
compareHints: Among its Suillus relatives, the Painted Suillus stands out dramatically with its red and yellow crackled cap pattern – most other slippery jacks have solid-colored, slimy caps in browns or yellows. While species like the Purple-veiled Slippery Jack (S. luteus) also have rings on their stems, none share that distinctive paint-peeling appearance. The dry, scaly texture also sets it apart from most Suillus species, which tend to have sticky or slimy cap surfaces.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Slippery Jacks, the Chicken Fat Mushroom stands out with its reddish-brown cap scales and consistently slimy texture - features that separate it from the Purple-veiled Slippery Jack's partial veil or the Dotted-stalked Suillus's white cap.
Unlike the Painted Suillus with its reddish streaks, or the Chicken Fat Mushroom with its more orange tones, the Butterball maintains consistent golden-butter coloring.
Unlike its cousin the Purple-veiled Slippery Jack which has a distinctive ring around the stem, the Dotted-stalked Suillus has a completely ringless stem covered in granular dots.
Among its Suillus relatives, Slippery Jill stands out with its distinctive reddish-brown dotted stem - most other slippery jacks either lack these glandular dots or have different colored ones.
